papers.title: Pathogen-specific positron emission tomography for Enterobacterales bone infection.
papers.abstract: Gram-negative bone infections involving Enterobacterales group of bacteria pose a growing concern, especially for orthopaedic surgeries and diabetic ulcers. Current imaging methods either identify morphological changes by CT and MRI, or inflammation, using white blood cell scans or 2-deoxy-2-[ 18 F]fluoro-d-glucose ([ 18 F]-FDG) positron emission tomography (PET). While valuable, these are not specific, resulting in delayed diagnoses. PET/CT using 2-deoxy-2-[ 18 F]fluoro-d-sorbitol ([ 18 F]-FDS) is a novel method for detecting living Enterobacterales bacteria in vivo, via a conserved sorbitol-specific bacterial pathway. In this study, we aim to evaluate [ 18 F]-FDS PET/CT for detection and monitoring of Enterobacterales bone infection in a mouse model. We adapted a murine model of Gram-positive implant-associated spine infection to a Gram-negative infection model. We compared microbiological techniques to imaging with [ 18 F]-FDG and [ 18 F]-FDS. We determined the standardized uptake value (SUV) ratios for detection of bacterial infection and response to therapy, in 48 mice with surgical implants infected with either Escherichia coli or Staphylococcus aureus and compared them to controls with surgical implants but no infection. Both bacteria induced substantial bone pathology with reduced bone density. [ 18 F]-FDS PET could specifically detect implant-associated spinal infections due to E. coli with a mean SUV ratio of 2.2 (SD 1.3), which was substantially lower in S. aureus (0.7 (SD 0.2); p = 0.002) and uninfected mice (1.0 (SD 0.1)). In contrast, [ 18 F]-FDG could not differentiate between the two bacterial infections or the control (p = 0.497). Finally, [ 18 F]-FDS PET could determine antibiotic efficacy, and monitor infection over time. We demonstrate that [ 18 F]-FDS affords a highly accurate and clinically translatable detection of Enterobacterales bone infection. This novel modality offers a rapid and specific method to diagnose and monitor bone infections, inform medical decisions, reduce the need for surgery, and limit unnecessary antibiotic use. Similar approaches may be implemented to develop tracers for other bacteria.

papers.title: A sequence-informed hybrid framework for predicting antibiotic minimum inhibitory concentrations in previously unseen Escherichia coli pathogens.
papers.abstract: When an Escherichia coli pathogen is newly encountered, antimicrobial susceptibility information may be incomplete or unavailable. We investigated whether minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) could be predicted for previously unseen pathogens by jointly using pathogen genomic sequence information, antibiotic characteristics, and observed pathogen-antibiotic MIC patterns. The predictive value of integrating pathogen genomic information, antibiotic characteristics, and observed pathogen-antibiotic MIC patterns within a hybrid collaborative-filtering framework for previously unseen E. coli pathogens remains unclear. To develop and evaluate Model C for predicting MIC values in previously unseen, genomically characterised E. coli pathogens. The study used 9377 E. coli pathogens, 26 antibiotics, and 51,554 exact MIC measurements among 243,802 possible pathogen-antibiotic combinations. Model C combined observed MIC patterns, genomic features related to antimicrobial resistance (AMR), nucleotide-sequence comparisons across 265 AMR-related loci, and antibiotic characteristics. Five-fold pathogen-out validation excluded all MIC measurements from each test pathogen from training and model selection. The common validation cohort contained 9058 pathogens and 50,460 observed MIC values; Models 3B and 3 were evaluated as comparators. In pathogen-out validation of the 50,460 observed MIC values, Model C achieved a mean absolute error of 0.5931 log₂ MIC units, root mean squared error of 0.8477, and Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.9055. Model C performed best overall. A final model fitted to all 50,460 observed MICs predicted the remaining 185,048 unmeasured MICs. Model C estimated MIC values for previously unseen E. coli pathogens using genomic, antibiotic, and observed interaction information. Independent external validation is required. Predictions may help prioritise confirmatory testing but should not replace antimicrobial susceptibility testing or be used alone to guide treatment.

papers.title: Mechanism Investigation of Platycodon grandiflorum Active Ingredients in Regulating Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition and Airway Remodeling in Asthma via Modulation of the Sirt6/RORγt/IL-17A Axis and IL-17A/MAPK Pathway.
papers.abstract: Platycodon grandiflorum (Jacq.) A.DC. is a traditional Chinese medicinal herb recognized for its dual role as both food and medicine, renowned for its effects of diffusing the lung, alleviating sore throat, promoting expectoration, and facilitating pus drainage. In traditional medicinal practice, it is often used in combination with herbs such as Ephedra sinica , Prunus armeniaca and Glycyrrhiza uralensis utilized to mitigate symptoms associated with asthma, bronchitis, and other respiratory diseases. However, the therapeutic effects and molecular mechanisms of its principal bioactive components in treating asthma remain insufficiently characterized. To investigate the pharmacological effects and elucidate the molecular mechanisms by which triterpenoid saponins derived from Platycodon grandiflorum (PL-TS) inhibit airway epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and attenuate airway remodeling in asthma. Initially, the chemical constituents of the triterpenoid saponin fraction extracted from Platycodon grandiflorum (Jacq.) A. DC. (PL-TS) were identified by Ultra Performance Liquid Chromatography Tandem Mass Spectrometry (UPLC-MS). Subsequently, network pharmacology approaches were employed to predict potential therapeutic targets and core signaling pathways of PL-TS in asthma. An OVA-induced asthmatic mouse model was established for in vivo experiments. Airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR) was assessed via whole-body plethysmography (WBP), and histopathological changes in lung tissues were examined via hematoxylin-eosin (HE), Masson's trichrome, and periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) staining. Human bronchial epithelial cells (BEAS-2B) were utilized to establish an IL-17A-induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) model in vitro. Finally, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), immunohistochemistry (IHC), quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), and Western blotting (WB) were employed to investigate the modulatory effects of PL-TS on proteins associated with airway remodeling, the IL-17A/MAPK signaling pathway, and the Sirt6/RORγt/IL-17A axis in both asthmatic mice and cellular models. UPLC-MS/MS analysis identified 38 triterpenoid saponins from PL-TS, providing a chemical foundation for subsequent mechanistic studies. Network pharmacology analysis revealed that the principal targets of PL-TS were predominantly enriched within the IL-17A signaling pathway. In OVA-induced asthmatic mice, PL-TS significantly attenuated inflammatory cell infiltration, mucus hypersecretion, and collagen deposition in lung tissues, while markedly reducing serum levels of IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, and OVA-IgE in vivo. Furthermore, PL-TS was found to inhibit the activation of the IL-17A/MAPK and Sirt6/RORγt/IL-17A signaling pathways in both mouse lung tissue and stimulated cells, while downregulating EMT-related protein Vimentin, Snail, and N-cadherin, upregulating expression of E-cadherin. suppressing the phosphorylation of p38, ERK, and JNK in the MAPK pathway. In addition, PL-TS downregulated Sirt6 expression and reduced RORγt and IL-17A levels, suggesting a potential involvement of the Sirt6/RORγt/IL-17A regulatory axis, although the precise epigenetic mechanism requires further investigation. This study demonstrated that the PL-TS significantly alleviated airway inflammation, mucus hypersecretion, and airway remodeling in asthma model. The effects were associated with suppression of the IL-17A/MAPK pathway and downregulation of the Sirt6/RORγt/IL-17A axis, suggesting a potential dual mechanism that highlight its therapeutic potential.

papers.title: Conversational Multi-Agentic Network-Driven Disease Module Identification and Drug Repurposing Prediction With ChatDRex: Platform Development Study.
papers.abstract: Repurposing approved drugs offers a time- and cost-effective alternative to traditional drug development. However, in silico prediction of repurposing candidates is challenging and requires the effective collaboration of specialists in various fields, including pharmacology, medicine, biology, and bioinformatics. Fragmented, specialized algorithms and tools often address only narrow aspects of the overall problem. Heterogeneous, unstructured data landscapes require the expertise of specialized users. Hence, diverse data sources might not integrate smoothly across workflows. We aimed to develop an integrated, natural language-driven system that enables domain experts to conduct complex network-based drug repurposing analyses by integrating heterogeneous biomedical data sources and specialized bioinformatics methods within a unified workflow. With ChatDRex, we present a conversation-based, multi-agent system that facilitates the execution of complex bioinformatic analyses aiming for network-based drug repurposing prediction. It builds on the integrated systems medicine knowledge graph NeDRexDB. ChatDRex provides natural language access to its extensive biomedical knowledge base. It integrates bioinformatics agents for network analysis, literature mining, and drug repurposing. These are complemented by agents that evaluate functional coherence for in silico validation. Its flexible multi-agent design assigns specific tasks to specialized agents, including query routing, data retrieval, algorithm execution, and result visualization. A dedicated reasoning module keeps the user in the loop and allows for hallucination detection. ChatDRex operationalizes complex network-based drug repurposing workflows through conversational interaction, integrating biomedical knowledge access with algorithm execution and validation-oriented assessments. Its modular multi-agent architecture enables scalable task specialization across retrieval, analysis, validation, and visualization, while the reasoning module provides transparency and safeguards against unreliable outputs. By enabling researchers with limited computational expertise to control complex analyses with natural language, ChatDRex could democratize access to bioinformatics as an important resource for drug repurposing. It could enable clinical experts to generate hypotheses and explore drug repurposing opportunities, ultimately accelerating the discovery of novel therapies and advancing personalized medicine and translational research.

papers.title: Multi-virus Wastewater Surveillance in Heterogeneous Urban-Sewage Systems: Comparative Insights From Sewage Treatment Plants and Open Drains.
papers.abstract: Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) has been applied for public health surveillance for several decades but gained unprecedented global prominence during the COVID-19 pandemic, leading to its broader adoption for multi-pathogen surveillance. However, the impact of heterogeneous urban wastewater infrastructure on the detection and interpretation of pathogen signals remains inadequately characterised, particularly in settings such as Mumbai, with fragmented and partially connected sewer networks. This study systematically compared multi-pathogen wastewater surveillance from centralised sewage treatment plants (STPs) and decentralised open drains (ODs), which represent aggregated and localised population catchments, respectively. Wastewater was collected during two monitoring periods (2023 and 2024) and analysed by RT-qPCR for SARS-CoV-2, influenza viruses, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Comparative analyses included detection frequency, temporal dynamics, and patterns of viral co-occurrence between node types. Viral detection rates were highest in STP influent, consistent with signal integration over larger populations and reduced short-term variability. Conversely, open drains exhibited greater temporal fluctuation, which may be consistent with localised, short-term changes but with reduced signal persistence. In the absence of concurrent clinical data, these node-level differences are interpreted as patterns in the wastewater signal rather than demonstrated gains in epidemiological sensitivity or earlier detection. SARS-CoV-2 was consistently detected across both node types, while influenza virus detection was more sporadic and exhibited marked variability, suggesting seasonal transmission dynamics. Co-detection of influenza A and B was observed in 2023, and influenza A subtyping revealed limited within-type diversity; source attribution for the detected subtypes could not be determined. Collectively, these findings indicate that wastewater signal profiles reflect an interplay between pathogen-specific characteristics and the structural configuration of the sampling network. Overall, the findings support integrated surveillance frameworks that leverage both centralised and decentralised nodes, while highlighting the need for extended temporal monitoring and independent clinical validation to strengthen epidemiological inference.

papers.title: Genomic rearrangement of the capsule operon in a phylogenetically distinct cluster of the multi-drug-resistant Escherichia coli lineage ST131.
papers.abstract: Escherichia coli ST131 is a dominant cause of multi-drug-resistant extraintestinal infections in humans. The lineage has a three-clade phylogenetic structure, of which clade C has gained resistance to multiple classes of antibiotics and is globally disseminated. As well as antimicrobial resistance, a number of virulence factors contribute to the success of ST131 clade C, including the production of capsule. Previous work on a limited number of strains has shown that the capsule operon in ST131 is highly variable. In this study, we analyzed the capsule genetics of E. coli ST131 by interrogating 3,033 genomes. Our data show a clonal distribution of capsule types and identify a monophyletic group of ST131 clade C strains that are characterized by an atypical capsule operon with highly divergent alleles of the key kpsM and kpsT genes. Our analysis suggests there is ongoing evolution within clade C of ST131, which looks to be driven not by the continuing evolution of antimicrobial resistance but by host-pathogen interactions.IMPORTANCEMulti-drug-resistant (MDR) Escherichia coli is a problematic cause of invasive disease in humans and animals. Resistance to multiple classes of antibiotics is severely limiting treatment options. ST131-C is a highly successful, MDR clone of E. coli that is a major cause of extraintestinal infections. Capsule is a key virulence factor in contributing to this clone's success, with capsule switching allowing the bacteria flexibility to thrive in different niches. We present evidence that suggests continual evolution of this proliferant clone influenced by host-pathogen interaction. Small genetic changes can define the success of a clone; therefore, it is important to monitor this continual evolution in pathogens.

papers.title: Enterobacteriaceae and Bacteriophages: Implications Against Antimicrobial Resistance.
papers.abstract: Enterobacteriaceae represent a clinically challenging bacterial family owing to the global emergence of multidrug resistance. Bacteriophages, the natural predators of these bacteria, have emerged as powerful tools for detecting, targeting, and inhibiting these pathogens. This review provides a comprehensive overview of bacteriophages targeting Enterobacteriaceae hosts, focusing on their diversity, virion architecture, and the molecular determinants of host specificity. The dynamic co-evolution between bacterial defence strategies and phage counter-defences is discussed to illustrate the complexity of the phage-Enterobacteriaceae host interactions. Translational applications of Enterobacteriaceae phages, including phage therapy, engineered phages, phage-derived lysins as antimicrobials, and phage-based diagnostics for rapid and specific pathogen detection is also explored alongside their limitations including limited large-scale clinical trials, regulatory and manufacturing hurdles, and the need for robust host-range prediction and standardization. Overall, this review elaborates implications of bacteriophage-Enterobacteriaceae interactions to combat antimicrobial resistance and support the development of next-generation antibacterial therapies and diagnostics.

papers.title: The LbBLH9-LbGeBP module regulates salt gland development and salt tolerance in Limonium bicolor.
papers.abstract: GLABROUS1 enhancer-binding protein (GeBP) transcription factors play pivotal roles in the regulating plant development and stress responses. However, the function of GeBP family members in regulating salt gland development and salt tolerance in Limonium bicolor remains unclear. In this study, the gene LbGeBP1 exhibited high expression levels during the early stages of salt gland development. We found that LbGeBP1 is mainly expressed in salt glands and LbGeBP1 localizes in the nucleus. Functional analysis through overexpression and knockout of LbGeBP1 in L. bicolor showed that LbGeBP1 negatively regulates salt gland development and salt tolerance. Further investigation revealed that the BEL1-like homeobox (BLH) LbBLH9 binds to the LbGeBP1 promoter and represses its expression. LbBLH9 was specifically expressed in salt glands. In contrast to LbGeBP1, LbBLH9 was found to positively regulate salt gland development and salt tolerance. Consistent with this regulatory relationship, silencing LbBLH9 in the LbGeBP1-overexpression background further increased LbGeBP1 expression and exacerbated defects in salt gland development and salt secretion. In contrast, simultaneous silencing of LbBLH9 and LbGeBP1 partially rescued the defects caused by silencing LbBLH9 alone. Together, these molecular and genetic data support a model in which LbBLH9 promotes salt gland development and salt tolerance by repressing the transcription of LbGeBP1. Furthermore, the LbBLH9-LbGeBP1 module regulates the expression of genes involved in salt gland development and salt stress responses. This study reveals a novel molecular mechanism governing salt gland development and salt tolerance in L. bicolor, providing a theoretical foundation for elucidating salt tolerance mechanisms in plants.

papers.title: Investigating the Distinctive Clinical and Genetic Landscape of PPA2 Deficiency.
papers.abstract: PPA2 encodes for inorganic pyrophosphatase 2, a mitochondrial enzyme that hydrolyzes inorganic pyrophosphates into orthophosphate. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause PPA2 deficiency, an emerging recessive cardiac condition that causes heart failure and sudden cardiac death in infants and young people. Using published case reports and large-scale genomics resources, we defined the clinical and molecular spectrum of this disease, classified variants using a customized American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics pipeline, assessed genotype-phenotype correlations, calculated predicted prevalence using the gnomAD GenIE tool, and investigated monoallelic associations in the UK Biobank. A total of 63 cases from 37 families were identified from 12 publications. The natural history of this disease is characterized by clinical heterogeneity and high mortality (79% by 20 years of age), typically presenting as a highly arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy with 2 distinct risk periods: in infancy, where viral infections can lead to heart failure, and in adolescence, where minimal alcohol exposure can trigger sudden cardiac death. The disease is genetically heterogeneous, with 29 distinct variants described (18 of which were classified as [likely] pathogenic), usually in compound heterozygosity. As complete gene knockout appears to be incompatible with life, PPA2 deficiency is caused by biallelic variants within a particular loss-of-function window, with deficiency mitigated by hypomorphic effects, variants in nonconstitutive exons, and particular compound heterozygous combinations. The spectrum of phenotypic effect extends to monoallelic carriers of pathogenic variants, which demonstrate an apparent mitohormesis-like compensatory protection from heart failure. The disease has an estimated prevalence of at least 1/135 000 in European ancestry populations. PPA2 deficiency is a genetically complex and clinically severe disease. Given the potential for effective life-saving interventions, PPA2 may warrant inclusion in emerging newborn genomic screening programs.

papers.title: KARS1-Related Infantile-Onset Progressive Leukoencephalopathy With or Without Deafness: A Novel Variant and Phenotypic Expansion.
papers.abstract: Biallelic variants in the KARS1 gene, encoding lysyl-tRNA synthetase, are responsible for autosomal recessive disorders such as infantile-onset progressive leukoencephalopathy with or without deafness (LEPID; OMIM #619147) and nonsyndromic hearing loss (DFNB89). Common features of LEPID include sensorineural hearing loss, developmental delay, and leukoencephalopathy, but dysmorphic facial features and cardiac anomalies are not commonly reported. This study presents the first documented LEPID case in Iran, expanding the phenotypic and genetic spectrum of KARS1-related disorders. Whole exome sequencing (WES) was performed on a two-year-old Iranian boy from non-consanguineous parents, without a positive history of any neurologic conditions. Identified variants were validated by Sanger sequencing, with familial segregation analysis. Moreover, a literature review of 41 KARS1-related cases was conducted to compare clinical and genetic findings. WES identified two compound heterozygous KARS1 variants (NM_005548.3): c.959G > A (p.Arg320His) and c.2T > C (p.Met1Thr), previously reported and novel, respectively, both of which were classified as likely pathogenic according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics criteria. The patient exhibited typical LEPID features (sensorineural hearing loss, developmental delay, seizures, leukoencephalopathy) alongside unprecedented dysmorphic facial features (e.g., synophrys, pointed triangular chin) and cardiac anomalies (pulmonary stenosis, atrial septal defect). Literature review confirmed these dysmorphic features as novel, absent in prior cases, with cardiac involvement in a limited number of patients. This study highlights a novel KARS1 variant and an expanded phenotypic spectrum of LEPID, emphasizing the role of WES in diagnosing rare disorders even in non-consanguineous marriages. These findings advocate for broader phenotypic recognition and functional studies to elucidate KARS1's role in neurodevelopmental, craniofacial, and cardiac abnormalities.

papers.title: Protein large language model-assisted one-to-one gene homology mapping in cross-species single-cell transcriptome integration.
papers.abstract: Cross-species integration of single-cell transcriptomes requires establishing gene correspondences to enable comparative analysis of expression profiles across organisms. Current approaches predominantly rely on Ensembl homology tables; although gene-family expansion and contraction can reflect biologically meaningful evolutionary divergence, default many-to-many mappings can overweight expanded gene-family signals during integration and generate mapping-associated microclusters that lack clear cell-type identity, thereby complicating direct cell-type alignment. Although restricting mappings to a one-to-one scheme suppresses such artifacts, it reduces the number of homology gene pairs by ∼8% (about 900 pairs). To address this limitation, we develop a protein large language model (pLLM)-based gene homology mapping strategy that boosts the number of homology gene pairs. By enforcing a one-to-one mapping constraint and integrating pLLM-derived representations with sequence similarity, we construct a fused mapping approach, which achieves top performance in a comprehensive benchmark based on a curated cross-species atlas spanning nine data sets, 11 species, and more than 3.2 million cells. Our method further identifies previously unannotated cell-type marker pairs, facilitating novel cross-species marker discovery. These results establish a robust framework for gene homology mapping in cross-species transcriptome integration, improving both accuracy and biological interpretability.

papers.title: Counting reactions, not just variants: what malignant hyperthermia can teach precision medicine.
papers.abstract: Susceptibility to malignant hyperthermia is generally considered to follow an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with incomplete penetrance. In a recent study in the British Journal of Anaesthesia, Aboelsaod and colleagues integrate national epidemiological data, anaesthetic exposure histories, population genomics, contracture test phenotyping, and Bayesian modelling to estimate the prevalence of individuals capable of developing clinical malignant hyperthermia. Their findings support a threshold model in which variants contribute different degrees of biological liability, potentially modified by other genetic and environmental factors, whereas the probability of reacting during a triggering exposure seems relatively similar once an individual has crossed this threshold. The study also illustrates how combining complementary sources of imperfect evidence can improve risk estimation for rare, exposure-dependent disorders. Ultimately, malignant hyperthermia genetics needs to move beyond categorical variant classification towards variant-specific penetrance estimates that incorporate genetic background, ancestry, exposure history, and other determinants of clinical expression.

papers.title: Identifying novel genomic alterations in relapsed childhood B-ALL: a report from the Children's Oncology Group.
papers.abstract: Relapsed B-acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) generally occurs due to the emergence of subclones resistant to therapy, leading to poor outcome. Here, we describe novel genomic alterations responsible for therapeutic resistance at a subtype level in a clinical trial (AALL1331) which randomized patients to blinatumomab and chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone. We performed whole-genome and transcriptome sequencing on 288 patients (183 diagnosis/first relapse/germline trios and 105 additional patients with first-relapse samples) and analyzed 41 second-relapse samples. For ETV6::RUNX1, we showed that cases with gain of the fusion allele or with fusion transcript involving exon 5 of ETV6 and exon 4 of RUNX1 (E5-E4) had a higher risk of first relapse than cases with E5-E3. For the hyperdiploid subtype, we demonstrated that low modal chromosomal numbers (51-52) were more prone to first relapse than those with ≥53 chromosomes, with an additive effect of CREBBP mutations. We showed enrichment of IKZF1 alterations in the Philadelphia-like subtype and that NSD2 E1099K was commonly associated with relapse in TCF3::PBX1. Together, these new features accounted for 30% (n=55) of first relapses. Intriguingly, ~3% of relapses are related to secondary B-ALL or germline predisposition. We also compared genomic alterations at diagnosis and first relapse in relation to second relapse status in randomized patients, with TCF3::PBX1/NT5C2 linked to worse outcomes regardless of randomized arm. Together, our findings provide novel insights into the genomics of relapsed childhood B-ALL as well as in the context of blinatumomab therapy. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as # NCT0201853.

papers.title: Enhancing pathogen detection in pediatric diarrheal stools: The case of molecular multiplexing with a real-time PCR assay.
papers.abstract: Diarrhea is a leading cause of pediatric morbidity and mortality worldwide, frequently caused by various bacterial, viral, and protozoan pathogens. Identification of these pathogens is important in clinical settings for proper management of the infection. Conventional stool culture technique is time-consuming for the detection of diarrheagenic pathogens. In addition, these traditional procedures lack sensitivity, require a specific laboratory structure, and well-trained staff. Conversely, multiplex molecular detection methods offer rapid results with less hands-on time and more sensitivity. This study compared the diagnostic performance of conventional microbiological methods and GastroFinder 2SMART multiplexed real-time PCR (real-time PCR) assay for detecting enteric pathogens in pediatric stool samples. Overall pathogen detection was significantly higher using this real-time PCR (81%) compared to the conventional assays (43.1%), reflecting differences in both sensitivity and pathogen panel breadth. Rotavirus, adenovirus, Shigella, and Giardia lamblia were frequently identified by conventional methods, whereas real-time PCR commonly detected adenovirus, Campylobacter, EPEC, ETEC, and norovirus. Certain pathogens such as Yersinia enterocolitica, Clostridioides difficile, STEC, and Dientamoeba fragilis were not tested in the conventional panel and therefore excluded for comparison. Sensitivity estimates varied, with lower sensitivity observed for EPEC, Cryptosporidium, G. lamblia, and rotavirus, partly due to the small sample numbers and wide confidence intervals. Specificity exceeded 90% for most pathogens, and diagnostic accuracy was > 90% for Shigella/EIEC, Salmonella, Cryptosporidium, Giardia lamblia, and astrovirus. Bayesian latent class analysis demonstrated the highest sensitivity for Shigella/EIEC (93.2%), followed by norovirus and adenovirus, while overall test performance, measured by the Youden Index, was greatest for Shigella/EIEC. These findings highlight the diagnostic use of real-time PCR and support its integration into routine diarrheal diagnostics to improve pathogen detection and clinical management.

papers.title: Impact of growth media on vancomycin susceptibility and mycobacterial cell wall integrity.
papers.abstract: Tuberculosis remains the leading cause of death by a single infectious agent, Mycobacterium tuberculosis , in the world. To tackle this disease, efforts are conducted, among others, to improve diagnosis coverage and treatment access, to develop an improved vaccine, and to find new antituberculous drugs or drug regimens. In vitro , bacteria usually tend to lose virulence factors to improve their fitness, mostly observed by an increased growth. This is also the case for M. tuberculosis strains and clinical isolates prone to lose phthiocerol dimycocerosates in the upper leaflet of their mycomembrane. This loss affects the cell wall integrity, as observed by an increased antimycobacterial activity of vancomycin, providing a potential bias in drug susceptibility testing. Here, we showed that M. tuberculosis culture conditions, such as a single subculture on 7H11 supplemented with oleic acid-albumin-dextrose-catalase, can restore vancomycin resistance and cell wall integrity but can also impact routine drug susceptibility assay by broth microdilution. Vancomycin susceptibility testing can identify Mycobacterium tuberculosis subcultures with compromised cell wall integrity due to phthiocerol dimycocerosates loss. A single pre-culture on potato-Sauton medium or on 7H11 supplemented with oleic acid-albumin-dextrose-catalase can restore cell wall integrity. This study underscores the importance of standardized culture protocols for reliable M. tuberculosis drug susceptibility testing.

papers.title: Mathematical modeling in mRNA therapeutics: towards a pathway to individualized treatment protocols.
papers.abstract: mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) therapeutics represent a transformative pharmacological paradigm in which the delivery vehicle, genetic payload, and expressed protein form a tightly coupled system. This multicomponent structure introduces nonlinear, multiscale dynamics that challenge traditional pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic frameworks, making quantitative modeling essential. This review provides a structured biological framework for mRNA-LNP therapeutics, detailing the key processes governing delivery, endosomal escape, mRNA stability, and translation, and highlighting their associated temporal and spatial scales, providing the key aspects to consider for modeling. Building on this foundation, we summarize mathematical modeling approaches, including pharmacokinetic (PK), pharmacodynamic (PD), physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK), and quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) models, used to represent these mechanisms. The literature was surveyed to identify representative preclinical and translational studies, focusing on model structure, assumptions, and their use in human projection and dose optimization. Mathematical models are increasingly critical to interpret and predict mRNA therapeutic behavior, yet challenges remain in parameter identifiability, data availability, and model standardization. Future advances will depend on biologically grounded modeling frameworks, improved integration of mechanistic insight with quantitative approaches, and tighter coupling between experimental design and model development. These developments will support more efficient translation and enable precision medicine applications.

papers.title: Harigabri-Derived Carbon Dots as FRET Probes for E. coli Analysis.
papers.abstract: Green-fluorescent carbon quantum dots (CQDs) were hydrothermally synthesized from the Mongolian medicine Harigabri, exhibiting uniform size (∼2.5 nm) and strong emission at 521 nm under 468 nm excitation. Based on the fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) between the CQDs (donors) and AgNPs (acceptors), an aptamer-functionalized biosensor (Apt-CQDs/AgNPs) was constructed for selective Escherichia coli detection. Target recognition by the aptamer inhibited FRET and restored fluorescence. The sensor showed a linear response from 9 × 102 to 9 × 107 CFU/mL with a detection limit of 5 CFU/mL. This work highlights Harigabri-derived CQDs as promising nanomaterials for rapid pathogen detection and demonstrates the potential of traditional medicinal resources in biosensing applications.

papers.title: Clinical and Molecular Spectrum of KBG Syndrome in the Largest Independent Turkish Cohort.
papers.abstract: KBG syndrome (OMIM #148050) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by haploinsufficiency of ANKRD11 on chromosome 16q24.3. Populations outside Western Europe and North America remain underrepresented in the literature, and cohorts that comprehensively evaluate both sequence variants and copy-number variants (CNVs) remain limited. To characterize the clinical and molecular spectrum of KBG syndrome associated with an identified ANKRD11 alteration in a Turkish multicenter cohort, investigate genotype-phenotype correlations, and assess the contributions of sequence variants and CNVs to disease diagnosis and variant interpretation. Multicenter, retrospective cohort study. We retrospectively evaluated the clinical, anthropometric, and molecular characteristics of 36 Turkish individuals with KBG syndrome and an identified ANKRD11 alteration (31 pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants and five variants of uncertain significance) who were recruited from multiple pediatric genetics centers. Molecular analyses included whole-exome sequencing, clinical exome sequencing, and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA). Variants were classified according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics/Association for Molecular Pathology guidelines. An exploratory genotype-phenotype analysis was performed by comparing truncating, non-truncating sequence variant, and CNV/deletion groups using Fisher's exact and Mann-Whitney U tests, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. The cohort comprised 22 males and 14 females (male-to-female ratio, 1.57:1). A total of 29 distinct ANKRD11 alterations were identified, including 25 sequence variants and four distinct 16q24.3 deletions. Truncating variants were predominant (n = 25), while 11 sequence variants and four distinct 16q24.3 deletions further expanded the known molecular spectrum of KBG syndrome. The recurrent variant c.1903_1907del (p.Lys635GlnfsTer26) was identified in three unrelated individuals, supporting exon 9 as a major mutational hotspot. All three missense variants were clustered within the C-terminal degron, consistent with the previously reported enrichment of pathogenic missense variants in this functionally important region. 16q24.3 deletions accounted for 19.4% (7/36) of cases, underscoring the diagnostic value of copy-number analysis in patients with suspected KBG syndrome. This study finding expand the clinical and molecular spectrum associated with ANKRD11 , provide further evidence supporting haploinsufficiency as the primary disease mechanism, and underscore the diagnostic importance of CMA in syndromic neurodevelopmental disorders. Furthermore, integrating our cohort data with published findings provides a practical framework for interpreting ANKRD11 variants, particularly those involving the 5' regulatory region and C-terminal missense variants.

papers.title: Factor-Augmented Neural Conditional Density Estimation with Application to Drug Response Prediction.
papers.abstract: High-dimensional pharmacogenomic data pair thousands of molecular features with hundreds of cancer cell lines, complicating conditional density estimation. We study factor-augmented CINDES, which estimates conditional response densities from principal-component scores through binary classification. For an honest pilot/main-sample construction, assuming fresh-score PCA recovery, we derive a risk bound separating conditional-density learning, PCA score error, and representation bias. This guarantee does not cover the implemented procedure, which reuses observations for PCA and CINDES. In favorable strong-factor simulations, PCA improved a fixed CINDES pipeline, but PCA-MDN achieved lower negative log-likelihood (NLL) and integrated L 1 error in the matched comparison. Stress tests showed losses from omitted response-relevant low-variance directions and weak factor recovery, with sample-size-dependent factor-count effects. Across all 692 eligible source-specific genomics of drug sensitivity in cancer (GDSC) units and five splits, mean held-out NLL was 1.5414 for PCA-CINDES, versus 1.5661 and 1.5557 for ElasticNet and PCA/Ridge Gaussian models; PCA-MDN was better at 1.5156. A previously fixed 35-unit audit favored PCA-CINDES over Raw-X CINDES (mean paired NLL difference - 0 . 178 ) and found lower measured computational cost. The evidence supports PCA compression when retained factors capture response information and are accurately estimated; it does not establish robustness to general nonlinear or nonfactor structures, or CINDES as the preferred second-stage estimator. The application concerns preclinical prediction rather than clinical utility.

papers.title: Microfluidic Profiling of an Immune Cell-Associated Extracellular Vesicle Signature for Active Tuberculosis Diagnosis and Treatment Monitoring.
papers.abstract: Rapid and accurate diagnosis of active tuberculosis (ATB) remains challenging, particularly in paucibacillary cases, where conventional pathogen detection often fails. Plasma extracellular vesicles carrying innate immune cell-associated surface proteins, termed tuberculosis-associated immune cell extracellular vesicles (TB-IEVs), were investigated as biomarkers of ATB and integrated into a multichannel microfluidic platform. Whole-blood transcriptome profiling of patients with ATB and healthy controls (HCs) enabled the systematic selection of four innate immune cell-associated surface markers (RAB8A, TYROBP, C3AR1 and LILRA2). Marker validation using a bead-based immunoprecipitation assay confirmed elevated TB-IEV levels in ATB plasma. This signature was implemented on an 8-channel microfluidic chip, enabling parallel fluorescence analysis of only 10 µL of plasma within 30 min. In a clinical cohort (25 patients with ATB and 24 HCs), the TB-IEV multichannel chip achieved an area under the curve of 0.98. The signature also distinguished ATB from other respiratory diseases (n = 40) with an AUC of 0.95 and provided complementary diagnostic information in ATB patients with negative results on individual conventional tests. Longitudinal monitoring showed markedly decreased TB-IEV levels following anti-tuberculosis treatment. Collectively, this work demonstrated the potential of TB-IEV profiling as a rapid, minimally invasive approach for ATB diagnosis and treatment monitoring.

papers.title: Deciphering Host Genomic Pathway Landscapes in Severe COVID-19 by Exome Sequencing of a Large Admixed Brazilian Cohort.
papers.abstract: The host genetic factors that resulted in the heterogeneous clinical outcomes of COVID-19 remained poorly understood, especially in admixed populations that are underrepresented in global genomic studies. In this study, we investigated the genetic landscape associated with COVID-19 severity using whole-exome sequencing data from 325 Brazilian individuals recruited between 2020 and 2023. To prioritize variants related to disease severity, we applied a machine learning framework combining Support Vector Machine - Recursive Feature Elimination and SHAP interpretation. This approach encompasses 25 variants that contributed to the model's discrimination between severe and non-severe cases (AUC = 0.94) in our cohort. Subsequently, logistic regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, principal components of ancestry, and significant comorbidities confirmed several loci associated with severity after correction for multiple testing (FDR < 0.05). The prioritized genes were grouped into biological axes, including mitochondrial bioenergetics, neuroimmune signaling, complement activation, and epithelial structural integrity. Variants in genes such as MUC16, SLC4A2, LAPS1, ARRDC2, and CCSER1 showed associations with disease severity. Furthermore, functional annotation using CADD and regulatory exploration using GTEx suggested that several loci may influence gene regulation in lung, immune, and neural tissues. Instead of implicating single causal variants, our findings highlight pathway-level genetic architectures that may contribute to the variability of the host response to COVID-19. These findings provide exploratory insights into potential host genetic pathways that may be involved in disease variability in admixed environments. However, replication in independent cohorts and functional validation are still needed.

papers.title: Genetic dissection of soybean cyst nematode HG type 2.5.7 resistance reveals a multilocus architecture and favorable alleles from both parents.
papers.abstract: Soybean cyst nematode (SCN; Heterodera glycines ) is a major pathogen affecting soybean production worldwide. Understanding the genetic architecture of SCN resistance can facilitate the identification and utilization of favorable resistance alleles. We investigated resistance to SCN HG type 2.5.7 using an F₂ population ( n = 184) and a recombinant inbred line (RIL; F₂:₇, n = 323) population derived from Longken336 × Kangxian12, together with seven additional F 2 populations. The eight F₂ populations exhibited broad transgressive phenotypic segregation, including progeny with female index (FI) values extending beyond the corresponding parental range. QTL analysis identified six FI-associated loci in the Longken336 × Kangxian12 F₂ population on chromosomes 6, 7, 8, 11, 17, and 18, explaining 4.9-17.0% of the phenotypic variance, with one exceeding the permutation-derived significance threshold. High-density mapping in the RIL population identified resistance-associated loci across 17 chromosomes, with individual loci explaining 2.8-33.5% of the phenotypic variance. Seven QTL were consistently detected across both RIL evaluations, including four that exceeded the corresponding permutation-derived significance thresholds in both RIL evaluations. QTL regions colocalizing with the known resistance loci Rhg1 and Rhg4 were detected, along with favorable alleles contributed by both parental, including the phenotypically susceptible Longken336. Transcriptomic profiling identified contrasting infection-responsive expression patterns in both parental genotypes and prioritized candidate genes within selected QTL regions. These results highlight differences in QTL detection between the F 2 and RIL populations and support a multilocus basis for resistance to SCN HG type 2.5.7, with favorable alleles contributed by both parental backgrounds. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11032-026-01735-9.

papers.title: Geographical patterns of bacterial enteropathogens in diarrheal cases: a meta-analysis and systematic review (1999-2024).
papers.abstract: Bacterial enteropathogens are a leading cause of diarrheal diseases worldwide, with varying geographical trends. Understanding their distribution over time is critical for public health interventions. This meta-analysis and systematic review synthesizes evidence on the prevalence and geographical patterns of bacterial enteropathogens in diarrheal cases from 1999 to 2024. A comprehensive search was conducted through PubMed, Science Direct, Web of Science, Google Scholar and Scopus for studies reporting bacterial pathogen detection in diarrheal cases. Data was extracted on pathogen prevalence, geographic region, and temporal trends. Random-effects meta-analysis was performed to estimate pooled prevalence, and subgroup analyses assessed regional and year variations. Of the 100 included studies n = 790,141 samples, 72,354 pathogens isolates and 24,276 bacterial isolates, global bacterial isolates show high prevalence (59.2%) with marked regional variation. Africa reports the highest rate (69.6%), followed by America (58.1%), Europe (50.5%), and Asia (45.5%). Our studies also revealed high prevalence of Salmonella (11.0%) in Asia, Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC, 17.6%) and Enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC, 12.3%) in America, similarly, Campylobacter 's dominance (27.5%) in Europe, while in Africa Shigella has recorded the highest prevalence (10.0%). Bacterial enteropathogen prevalence exhibits significant geographical and temporal heterogeneity, influenced by socioeconomic and environmental factors. Targeted surveillance and region-specific interventions are needed to mitigate diarrheal disease burdens globally.

papers.title: Rapid RPA-Cas12a Assay for Streptococcus agalactiae Serotype III in Fish Featuring Photocontrolled One-Pot Detection.
papers.abstract: Streptococcus agalactiae is a primary pathogen responsible for significant mortality in tilapia, a critical and affordable source of animal protein. Among the various serotypes affecting aquaculture, serotype III is increasingly recognized for its high virulence and zoonotic potential, with multidrug resistance reported in some lineages. However, diagnostic tools that combine serotype-level resolution with field-deployability remain scarce. In this study, we developed a rapid and specific CRISPR-based detection platform targeting the cpsH gene of S. agalactiae serotype III. Combining recombinase polymerase amplification and CRISPR detection, the standard two-step RPA-Cas12a assay achieved a limit of detection (LoD) of 100 copies per reaction, with no cross-reactivity observed against closely related cpsH homologues from serotypes Ia, Ib and VI. The entire workflow can be completed within 1 h at a constant temperature of 37°C, providing visual readouts that can be easily and unambiguously interpreted. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the assay can be streamlined into a photocontrolled one-pot format, which reduces the risk of aerosol contamination while maintaining the same sensitivity as the two-step protocol. When evaluated against simulated DNA-spiked samples and field samples, both assay formats exhibited 100% concordance with each other and with the conventional PCR method, highlighting the potential of this platform as a step toward rapid, serotype-specific surveillance in aquaculture.

papers.title: Combination of canagliflozin and adagrasib as a novel targeted therapy for LKB1-KRAS G12C co-mutated NSCLC.
papers.abstract: In recent years, significant progress has been made in developing targeted therapy for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, these therapies are only applicable to specific NSCLC groups with corresponding gene mutations. Therefore, developing novel targeted therapies to benefit more patients remains an important task. Our prior work demonstrated that LKB1-mutant NSCLC cells are highly susceptible to cell death induced by glucose starvation. In this study, we investigated a novel combinational therapeutic strategy utilizing a sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor canagliflozin and a covalent KRAS G12C inhibitor adagrasib, two clinically approved therapeutics, to selectively target LKB1-KRAS G12C co-mutated NSCLC. First, we verified the co-occurrence of LKB1 and KRAS mutations in clinical NSCLC cohorts. Second, compared to other SGLT2 inhibitors, canagliflozin induced higher cytotoxicity in LKB1-mutant cells, and SGLT2 knockdown partially attenuated this effect. Mechanistically, the high susceptibility to canagliflozin was associated with impaired activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK). Furthermore, canagliflozin suppressed mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) activity and robustly inhibited cell growth in LKB1-mutant models in vitro. Third, adagrasib exhibited selective cytotoxicity in KRAS G12C -mutated NSCLC. Finally, the combination of canagliflozin and adagrasib synergistically reduced cell viability in LKB1-KRAS G12C co-mutated H23 and H2122 cells in vitro. Importantly, canagliflozin attenuated the adaptive MAPK signaling rebound induced by adagrasib in vitro. The therapeutic potential of this combination was confirmed in an H2122 nude mouse xenograft model in vivo. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that a combination of canagliflozin and adagrasib suppresses LKB1-KRAS G12C co-mutated NSCLC, laying a solid preclinical foundation for developing a new therapeutic strategy for this group of NSCLC.

papers.title: Genomic and phenotypic characterization of a honey-derived Enterococcus faecium isolate from the Brazilian semiarid region.
papers.abstract: Enterococcus faecium has attracted considerable scientific interest. While some strains are recognized as opportunistic nosocomial pathogens, several non-pathogenic isolates have demonstrated beneficial properties associated with food fermentation and probiotic potential. Therefore, this study aimed to perform a functional genomic characterization of the native E. faecium strain EFBI58, isolated from honey in the Brazilian semiarid region. Enterococcus faecium strain EFBI58 was sequenced using Illumina MiSeq. Bioinformatic tools were employed for comparative genomics, phylogeny, and detection of resistance, virulence, prophage, CAZyme, and bacteriocin genes. Additionally, in vitro tests assessed antimicrobial susceptibility and survival under simulated gastrointestinal conditions. The EFBI58 genome presented 2,457,210 base pairs, containing 2,330 coding sequences. Phylogenomic analyses demonstrated that honey-derived isolates formed a genetically distinct group. The ANI showing belonging to clade A2 of animal-associated species. Antimicrobial resistance assessment revealed the absence of acquired genes related to clinical resistance, which was confirmed by the phenotypic susceptibility profile to the evaluated antibiotics. In addition, genes associated with important virulence factors were not identified. A prophage was 21 kb also identified in the genome. The strain EFBI58 showed survival capacity under simulated gastrointestinal conditions and the presence of stress-response proteins, demonstrating mechanisms of adaptation to adverse environments. The profile of carbohydrate-active enzymes and growth in prebiotics sugars revealed a conserved metabolic repertoire associated with the utilization of different substrates. Honey- and bee-associated E. faecium isolates possess genomic characteristics that provide a basis for future investigations involving natural antimicrobial compounds, microbial interactions, and biotechnological applications.
authors: Maria Cecília de Lima E Silva

papers.title: Australian Standards of Care for Genetic and Genomic Testing in Kidney Disease.
papers.abstract: Genetic and genomic testing can refine diagnosis, prognosis, treatment, transplant assessment and family counselling for kidney disease, yet access remains uneven across Australia. These National Kidney Genomics Guidelines define a standard of care for genetic and genomic testing in nephrology and support the mainstreaming of genomic care while maintaining quality, governance and equity. The guidelines were developed by the KidGen Collaborative, comprising nephrologists, clinical geneticists, genetic counsellors, diagnostic laboratories, scientists and consumer advocates, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander representatives. They underwent open review. Recommendations are graded by strength and by the quality of evidence. The document covers governance and multidisciplinary models; patient selection and phenotyping; clinical indications, including transplantation; test selection; consent; requesting and funding; interpretation of results; post-test management and re-analysis; familial variant testing; and patient and clinician support. Equitable access for rural and remote communities, culturally and linguistically diverse groups, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples is prioritised. Predictive testing of asymptomatic relatives and testing of children without immediate medical benefit should be conducted through specialised genetics services. Variants of uncertain significance should not guide management. The guidelines are intended for nephrologists, clinical geneticists, genetic counsellors and health-service decision-makers, and will be reviewed every three to five years, or sooner if practice-changing evidence emerges.

papers.title: Interpretable Drug-Target Prediction via Geometric Alignment: A Linear Alternative to Deep Architectural Complexity.
papers.abstract: Designing selective kinase inhibitors is a multiobjective optimization problem constrained by the structural conservation of the human kinome, along with the lack of high-quality interaction data. Traditional deep learning methods often train complex neural networks directly on small datasets and fail to generalize to new chemical scaffolds. To this end, we present Geometric Manifold Alignment, a novel linear approach that shifts away from architectural complexity. We introduce Multi-View Linear Manifold (MVLM), which aligns the latent spaces of ChemBERTa (small molecules) and ESM-2 (protein sequences) into a shared geometric interaction space. We pretrain MVLM on the Universal Foundation Set of 473 923 high-confidence interactions, where binding affinity is represented as geometric proximity between drug and target embeddings. Achieving an AUROC of 0.936 on KIBA and 0.928 on Davis, MVLM establishes the new state-of-the-art on industry-standard benchmarks, outperforming existing methods (p < 0.001). In this work, interpretability is geometric where interaction scores are cosine similarities in a shared manifold, and the learned structure recovers kinase phylogenetic relationships without supervision. We also demonstrate the model's utility as a transparent discovery engine by retrieving known clinical targets of FDA-approved drugs. Our findings suggest that aligning pretrained chemical and biological representations provides a scalable and interpretable approach to advancing computational drug discovery.

papers.title: Exploring genetic variants in premature ovarian insufficiency: a cohort-based investigation of monogenic etiologies.
papers.abstract: Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), affecting about 3.5% of women under 40, is marked by menstrual irregularities, amenorrhea, and heterogeneous pubertal development. Although next-generation sequencing (NGS) has expanded the list of POI-associated genes, most cases remain unexplained, and the clinical diagnostic value of gene panels is still insufficiently assessed. This study combines a cohort-based analysis with a critical methodological reassessment of NGS diagnostic yield in POI. Prospective multicenter observational cohort study (2016-2023). Three Belgian academic hospitals. One hundred sixty unrelated women with idiopathic POI and 716 female controls. Targeted NGS of 155 POI-associated genes. Variants were classified following American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics/Association for Molecular Pathology guidelines, and genes were evaluated using the latest gene-disease relationship (GDR) scoring framework. Identification of pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants (primary outcome). Diagnostic yield of the gene panel based on genes with strong evidence (secondary outcome). Pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants were identified in 19.3% of patients; however, only 7.5% were considered clinically relevant based on gene validity and inheritance patterns. Limiting analysis to the 40 genes with the strongest GDR evidence yielded a 4.4% diagnostic rate. Adding 10 genes supported by recent literature increased the yield to 7.5%. In patients with primary amenorrhea, the diagnostic rate reached 15.4%. These findings highlight the gap between variant burden and true diagnostic yield in POI. Targeted NGS panels provide valuable clinical insight into POI genetics but should be complemented with broader genomic approaches for comprehensive diagnosis.

papers.title: Nipah Virus (NiV) in Focus: Molecular Insights Into Pathogenesis, Transmission Dynamics, and Evolving Epidemiology From Malaysia to Recent Indian Outbreaks.
papers.abstract: Since the emergence of the Nipah virus (NiV) in Malaysia in 1998, it has returned multiple times and continues to pose a significant threat to global public health. It is characterised by high mortality and fatality rates and increasing evidence of human-to-human transmission. The epidemiological pattern of NiV has shifted considerably over the past 2 decades, from transmission primarily associated with infected pigs to repeated spillover events linked to Pteropus fruit bats, contaminated food sources, and close human contact. NiV infection is marked by severe respiratory involvement, immune dysregulation, acute encephalitis and widespread endothelial damage contributing to rapid clinical deterioration and poor outcomes. The World Health Organisation classified the Nipah virus as a priority pathogen with high mortality and pandemic potential, with recognised outbreaks showing case fatalities ranging from 40% to 100%. The virus has been detected in the Indian subcontinent and is carried by fruit bats. Recent outbreaks reported in India through 2026 have further highlighted the ongoing threat posed by the virus and the challenges of outbreak containment in densely populated regions. Current advances in serological and Molecular diagnostics have improved early detection; however, therapeutic options remain limited, and no licenced vaccine is currently available for human use. Ongoing therapeutics research involving monoclonal antibodies, recombinant vaccines, and antiviral agent platforms continues to expand the prospects for future prevention and disease control. Outbreaks must be prevented by prompt diagnosis and the application of infection control measures. However, the lack of knowledge regarding the pathophysiology, clinical features, and current treatment of Nipah virus disease makes it difficult to design such trials. The current advances summarised herein strengthen the scientific foundation for improved diagnostic platforms, antiviral interventions, vaccine development, and integrated One Health surveillance approaches targeting Nipah Virus.

papers.title: Zinc Oxide and Graphitic Carbon Nitride/ZnO Nanocomposites in Food Safety and Preservation: Synthesis, Antimicrobial Mechanisms, and Application Prospects.
papers.abstract: Foodborne disease remains a major global health and economic burden, with recent World Health Organization estimates attributing roughly 866 million illnesses and 1.52 million deaths annually to 42 major foodborne hazards. Conventional preservation and decontamination strategies are increasingly challenged by antimicrobial-resistant pathogens, chemical residues, and mycotoxin contamination, creating demand for complementary nanotechnology-based interventions. Zinc oxide (ZnO) nanoparticles and their heterojunctions with graphitic carbon nitride (g-C 3 N 4 ) have emerged as versatile platforms combining broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity with visible-light-driven photocatalytic detoxification. This review synthesizes recent literature on the synthesis of ZnO nanoparticles by conventional and green/biogenic routes, including microbially mediated synthesis using actinobacteria such as Streptomyces species, and on the design of g-C 3 N 4 /ZnO S-scheme heterojunctions that suppress charge-carrier recombination while preserving strong redox potentials. We examine the principal antimicrobial and photocatalytic mechanisms-reactive oxygen species generation, Zn 2+ ion release, and direct membrane interaction-and their translation into food-relevant applications, including antimicrobial active packaging films and coatings, photocatalytic degradation of mycotoxins and pesticide residues, and nanomaterial-based biosensors for pathogen and spoilage detection. Toxicological and regulatory considerations, including nanoparticle migration from food-contact materials and evolving European Food Safety Authority and United States Food and Drug Administration frameworks, are discussed alongside persistent gaps in standardized safety testing, scale-up reproducibility, and life-cycle assessment. We conclude by outlining research priorities-particularly the systematic evaluation of biogenic ZnO and g-C 3 N 4 /ZnO composites under real food matrices and regulatory-relevant conditions-needed to advance these materials from laboratory demonstration toward safe, standardized, and sustainable adoption across the food value chain.

papers.title: Candidozyma auris (formerly Candida auris ): A P6 medicine framework integrating genomics, surveillance and the prevention of multidrug-resistant fungal threats.
papers.abstract: Healthcare-associated infections are major drivers of global morbidity; yet, fungal threats remain under-characterized. Candidozyma auris ( C. auris ; formerly known as Candida auris ) has emerged as a critical public health challenge due to its extensive multidrug-resistant profile, environmental resilience and high transmissibility. Its resistance to major antifungal classes, including azoles, polyenes and echinocandins, severely limits therapeutic options and exposes the limitations of fragmented, discipline-specific healthcare responses. The present conceptual commentary proposes that the persistence of C. auris highlights limitations in fragmented, discipline-specific healthcare responses. Herein, the predictive, preventive, personalized, participatory, psycho-cognitive and public (P6) model of medicine is proposed as a comprehensive framework to move beyond reactive containment. By repositioning clinical microbiology as the entry point for surveillance through early, accurate diagnosis, the P6 model integrates genomic epidemiology, antifungal stewardship and behavioral science to support earlier detection of emerging threats and inform timely clinical, infection prevention and control, and public health responses. The emergence of C. auris provides a practical test of the ability of healthcare systems to integrate microbiological intelligence, prevention strategies and public-health governance by replacing delayed laboratory identification, fragmented surveillance, or poor data sharing. Addressing its high resistance and rapid spread requires an integrative approach that leverages advanced analytics and public health governance. The P6 framework provides a scalable strategy to strengthen health systems against both current and future multidrug-resistant fungal pathogens.

papers.title: Generative artificial intelligence in medical oncology: A clinically focused narrative review of large language, vision-language, and agentic artificial intelligence systems.
papers.abstract: Rapid advances in cancer genetics and genomics, pathophysiology, diagnostics, and therapeutics have substantially increased the complexity of clinical oncology. Integrating large and diverse data streams into timely, patient-specific decisions provides a compelling rationale for incorporating artificial intelligence (AI) into cancer care. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) encompasses several classes of models capable of generating new content. This clinically focused review concentrates on GenAI applications based primarily on large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), as well as emerging agentic systems that use these models to perform coordinated, multistep tasks. LLMs demonstrate substantial medical knowledge, strong performance on oncology-related assessments, and emerging capabilities in clinical reasoning. Guideline- and retrieval-augmented systems can improve concordance with expert recommendations and interpretation of complex treatment algorithms. LLMs and VLMs have been applied to documentation, patient communication, information extraction and summarization, clinical decision support, and multimodal data synthesis. However, performance varies substantially across tasks and clinical domains, with important limitations including incomplete or outdated information, training-data bias, automation bias, and confabulation. Agentic AI represents an emerging extension of these technologies in which LLMs or VLMs are incorporated into systems capable of multistep planning, external information retrieval, specialized tool use, and iterative evaluation and refinement. Early oncology applications include evidence synthesis, multimodal clinical decision support, radiology, pathology, surgery, and individualized treatment planning. With rigorous validation, transparent implementation, continual updating, and appropriate expert oversight, GenAI may augment oncologists' judgment, improve patient understanding and experience, streamline cancer care delivery, and advance personalized oncology.

papers.title: CryoQSeg: robust particle segmentation for cryo-EM with Qwen-Image-Edit.
papers.abstract: Accurate particle picking remains a critical step in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) single-particle analysis, and the field has witnessed the development of a broad spectrum of approaches - from classical template-based methods to modern deep learning frameworks - to address this task. Here we present CryoQSeg, a particle segmentation and picking framework that represents a paradigm shift toward leveraging a state-of-the-art visual large model. Built upon Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 as its core backbone, CryoQSeg is fine-tuned through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on the public CryoPPP benchmark dataset, enabling the generation of high-fidelity, pixel-level particle masks directly from raw micrographs. To translate these masks into precise particle coordinates, we further integrate a hybrid post-processing pipeline that couples Hough circle detection with the segment anything model, forming a seamless end-to-end workflow from raw image input to accurate localization. We evaluate CryoQSeg on five representative benchmark datasets, demonstrating competitive performance across a range of protein types and imaging conditions in comparison to mainstream methods including Topaz and CryoSegNet. Furthermore, we validate the framework on the heterogeneous Crt-SPARTA-gRNA-tDNA complex, where it successfully resolves three distinct oligomeric states - monomer, dimer and tetramer - at high resolutions, despite using a fraction of the micrographs employed in the original study. By bridging modern visual large models with classical and foundation-model-based post-processing strategies, CryoQSeg demonstrates the potential of this emerging paradigm to deliver a robust and automated solution for cryo-EM particle picking, thereby contributing to a solid foundation for high-resolution three-dimensional structural determination of biological macromolecules.

papers.title: Validation of a MALDI Intact Cell Mass Spectrometry Workflow for Routine Application in Monitoring Industrial E. coli Fermentations.
papers.abstract: Today, matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization-intact cell mass spectrometry (MALDI-ICMS) is used in clinical environments for rapid pathogen identification, referred to as MALDI biotyping. This method relies on the generation of characteristic mass spectrometric profiles of intact microorganisms. Single-celled organisms are often used for pharmaceutical production, while this allows for the production of complex products, close monitoring and control of these processes is essential. In this study, we propose the use of MALDI-ICMS as a potential at-line approach for fast monitoring of the progress of a biotechnologically relevant fermentation process employing E. coli as a host. We demonstrate the reproducibility of the method, thereby indicating its potential to predict the progress of antibody fragment production in E. coli in an industrial setting. We evaluated various aspects of sample preparation, including the choice of matrix and solvent concentration, sample loading, and sample-to-matrix ratios. Our workflow allowed monitoring of over 100 signals across a 32-h span of E. coli fermentation. To control instrumental variability, we performed eight technical replicates and achieved excellent repeatability, with 9% median relative standard deviation of peak intensities. Principal component analysis revealed strong time-related differences of the mass spectra, allowing to differentiate the data based on fermentation phases. Furthermore, to assess direct monitoring of product expression, we adapted acquisition parameters to enable product detection via MALDI-ICMS. The presented MALDI-ICMS workflow allowed reliable monitoring of cellular changes during fermentation, thereby expanding the applications of MALDI-ICMS to process analytical technologies (PAT).

papers.title: Whole-exome sequencing of schizophrenia in an underrepresented indigenous population of Northeast India: Rare coding variant burden and clinical correlates.
papers.abstract: Schizophrenia is a severe mental disorder, and emerging evidence suggests that neurodevelopmental and synaptic dysfunction are critical factors in the pathogenesis of the disorder. This study investigated schizophrenia-related genetic variation in the genetically distinct and endogamous Mizo population of Northeast India using whole-exome sequencing. Twenty individuals with schizophrenia and 27 healthy controls were analysed. A panel gene consisting 95 gene associated with schizophrenia was initially used for descriptive profiling and pathway dysregulation, whereas an expanded 239-gene neuropsychiatric panel was used for standardized case-control analysis, recurrent and clinically significant variants and rare damaging effects. The descriptive analysis identified 321 variants across 32 genes, with recurrent variants most frequently observed in PCLO and RELN (100%), NRG1 (95%), CACNA1B (90%), BRCA1 (85%), and APOE and PLXNA2 (80%). Pathogenicity analysis revealed recurrent variants with conflicting pathogenic classifications in CNTNAP2, VDR, APOE, CHD8, and ERBB4. In the standardized case-control analysis, patients carried a significantly higher burden of rare damaging coding SNVs than controls. The synaptic burden score was positively correlated with PANSS negative-symptom severity, whereas its association with PANSS positive symptoms was not significant. Pathway analysis highlighted significant involvement of MAPK signalling, dopaminergic synapse, neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction and GABAergic synapse pathways. Overall, this first whole-exome study of schizophrenia in the Indigenous Mizo population provides preliminary evidence of increased rare damaging coding-variant burden and negative-symptom severity, supporting the involvement of synaptic and neurodevelopmental disturbances in an underrepresented Indigenous population.

papers.title: Biofilm-Mediated Persistence of Salmonella in Poultry Processing: A Comprehensive Review of Isolate Heterogeneity, Stress Adaptation, and Antimicrobial Resistance.
papers.abstract: Salmonella enterica remains a major foodborne pathogen in poultry-processing environments, where its persistence is largely attributed to biofilm formation on food-contact and non-food-contact surfaces. Despite extensive research on Salmonella control, persistent contamination continues to challenge food safety due to the complex interplay among isolate-specific traits, stress adaptation, and antimicrobial resistance (AMR). This review critically examines the phenotypic and genotypic determinants associated with Salmonella biofilm formation and evaluates their contributions to persistence, stress adaptation, and AMR. Emerging evidence also indicates that mixed-species interactions, particularly with Pseudomonas spp., can influence biofilm architecture, stress tolerance, and the long-term persistence of Salmonella in poultry-processing environments. Particular attention is given to processing-associated stresses, including temperature fluctuations, desiccation, nutrient limitation, and sublethal sanitizer exposure, which can induce adaptive responses that enhance biofilm development, promote persistence, and increase tolerance to antimicrobial interventions. The review further evaluates current detection approaches, including viability-based quantification methods such as digital droplet PCR, and discusses their limitations and applications in identifying and quantifying biofilm-associated and viable but nonculturable (VBNC) populations within processing environments. Existing control measures are assessed with emphasis on the challenges posed by mature biofilms and adaptive resistance mechanisms. Emerging antibiofilm technologies, including enzymatic treatments, bacteriophages, and UV-LED systems, are also examined for their potential industrial implementation. By integrating current knowledge on biofilm biology, stress adaptation, and AMR, this review provides a framework for developing targeted and sustainable strategies to mitigate Salmonella persistence in poultry-processing environments.

papers.title: Absence of BVDV infection in free-ranging ungulates supports BVD-free status in northeastern Germany.
papers.abstract: Bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV) is a major pathogen of cattle worldwide, for which control programs have been implemented in several countries. In Germany, long-term compulsory eradication measures have resulted in a marked decline of BVDV prevalence. Numerous federal states, among them Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, have achieved an official BVD-free status in domestic cattle. As wildlife may represent a potential source of virus reintroduction, this study investigated the occurrence of pestiviruses in free-ranging ungulates in this federal state between 2023 and 2025. Blood samples and nasal swabs from 909 animals, including roe deer, red deer, fallow deer, mouflon and wild boar, were analyzed using serological and molecular methods. All blood samples tested negative for antibodies against ruminant pestiviruses, and all ruminant nasal swabs were negative in two independent pan-pestivirus RT-PCR assays. One wild boar sample, however, tested positive by RT-PCR and the atypical porcine pestivirus (APPeV) was identified. The results provide evidence that free-ranging ungulates do not play a significant role in maintaining BVDV in regions, where the virus has been eradicated from domestic cattle. Nevertheless, sustained surveillance of wildlife remains important, particularly in regions with high wildlife density and close interactions between wildlife and livestock, to ensure early detection of potential reintroduction events or emerging pestiviruses, such as APPeV.

papers.title: Development of a recombinase-aided amplification assay for rapid and sensitive detection of Pneumocystis jirovecii infection: A single-center molecular study.
papers.abstract: Pneumocystis jirovecii (PJ) is a major opportunistic pathogen that causes severe pneumonia in immunocompromised individuals, leading to significant morbidity and mortality. Early and accurate diagnosis is critical for effective clinical management. However, existing diagnostic methods have limitations such as low sensitivity, long turnaround time and high equipment requirements. Recombinase-aided amplification (RAA) is an isothermal nucleic acid amplification technology with advantages of rapidity, simplicity and high sensitivity. The aim of this study was to develop and validate an RAA assay for the rapid detection of PJ. Clinical bronchoalveolar lavage fluid samples were collected from 44 PJ-positive patients confirmed by targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) and extracted nucleic acid. A recombinant PJ plasmid (pUC57-PJ) was constructed as the standard positive template. Specific primers and probes for PJ were designed and the RAA reaction conditions were optimized. The analytical performance (sensitivity, specificity) of the RAA method was evaluated using pUC57-PJ and clinical sample nucleic acids. Additionally, the clinical performance of RAA was validated by comparing with tNGS and RAA results. In conclusion, a rapid, sensitive and specific RAA assay for PJ detection was successfully developed. This assay exhibits excellent analytical and clinical performance, and is suitable for rapid diagnosis of PJ infection, particularly in resource-limited settings. It provides a valuable new tool for the early diagnosis and management of PJ pneumonia.

papers.title: Application of lytic bacteriophages OM982647 and OM982646 individually and in combination for mitigating STEC Escherichia coli O157:H7 in milk, yoghurt, and white soft cheese.
papers.abstract: Shiga toxigenic Escherichia coli (STEC O157:H7), a significant foodborne pathogen linked to dairy products, cause severe hemorrhagic enteritis in human. Nonetheless, the growing demand for natural, clean label and sustainable biocontrol food safety interventions has highlighted bacteriophages as promising biocontrol agents. In this study, the biocontrol efficacy of two lytic bacteriophages (STEC P2 and STEC P4) individually and in cocktail was evaluated against STEC O157:H7 in various dairy matrices (pasteurized milk, yoghurt, and white soft cheese). Coupled with assessing phages stability in cheese manufacturing conditions, and their potential impact on the starter culture activity. The findings revealed that, the phage cocktail (multiplicity of infection; MOI 10 6 ) eliminated STEC in milk within 2 h at 25 °C; however, bacterial regrowth was observed after 12 h.
